14640: "Sizable" means large enough to be worth noticing or taking seriously. It describes something that is not just a little big — it is big in a way that clearly stands out and actually matters.
Picture a scale

Imagine size on a spectrum:

tiny → small → medium → large → huge → enormous

"Sizable" sits toward the large end of this spectrum, but it does not mean the absolute biggest thing possible. It means: bigger than average, big enough that you cannot ignore it or dismiss it as small.
The heart of the word: "big enough to matter"

When you call something sizable, you are really saying three things at once:

  • It is not trivially small.
  • It is not a negligible amount.
  • It is big enough that a reasonable person would take notice.

A sizable amount of money → not a few coins, but a sum worth paying attention to.
A sizable crowd → not just a handful of people, but enough that you would call it a real crowd.
A sizable difference → not a minor gap, but a gap that is clearly noticeable.
It is a relative word — context decides what counts as "sizable"

This is one of the most important things to understand about "sizable." It does not describe the same absolute size in every situation. What counts as sizable depends entirely on what you are measuring and what is normal for that thing.

  • A sizable insect might be 5 cm long — which would be tiny for a building, but genuinely big for a bug.
  • A sizable salary might be ₹1.5 crore per year — large for most people, but perhaps unremarkable compared to a billionaire's income.
  • A sizable city might have one million people — massive for a small country, perfectly ordinary in India.

So "sizable" always means: large relative to what is normal or expected in that particular context.
How it feels — the tone of the word

"Sizable" has a calm, measured, slightly formal tone. It is not dramatic. It is not exaggerating. When someone uses it, they are being matter-of-fact — simply acknowledging that something is notably large, without making a big fuss about it.

Compare these two sentences:

  • "She made a massive profit." → Dramatic, perhaps a little exaggerated.
  • "She made a sizable profit." → Calm, credible, grounded — just stating a notable fact.

This is why "sizable" is a favourite in business reports, news writing, and professional conversation. But it also sounds perfectly natural in everyday speech. It is a versatile word that works in both formal and informal settings.
Examples across different situations

Amounts and quantities:

  • "The charity received a sizable donation from an anonymous supporter."
  • "He saved a sizable portion of his income every month."

Physical size:

  • "They moved into a sizable house on the edge of the city."
  • "There is a sizable crack in the ceiling that needs to be fixed."

Groups and crowds:

  • "A sizable crowd had gathered outside the concert hall."
  • "A sizable number of students did not pass the examination."

Differences and gaps:

  • "There is a sizable gap between his promises and his actions."
  • "The two bids had a sizable difference in price."

Share or portion of something:

  • "The company owns a sizable share of the market."
  • "A sizable chunk of the budget was spent on advertising."
An important nuance: vague by design

"Sizable" is intentionally imprecise about the exact size — and this is not a flaw. It is exactly how the word is meant to work. It allows a speaker to say "this is notably large" without committing to an exact number or making a precise comparison.

For example: "He inherited a sizable fortune" tells you the fortune is big and worth noting, but it says nothing about how many crores it is. The speaker is making a qualitative statement — a statement about the nature of the size — rather than a quantitative one.

This built-in vagueness is what makes "sizable" so useful. You can emphasize that something is genuinely large without overstating it, without exaggerating, and without needing precise data.
Words with similar meaning (synonyms)

Understanding similar words will sharpen your sense of exactly where "sizable" sits.

  • Considerable — the closest synonym; almost interchangeable with "sizable" in most sentences; slightly more formal.
  • Substantial — also very close; carries a slight added sense of solidity and weight, as if the size has real substance to it.
  • Significant — means the size is important or consequential, not just big.
  • Decent (informal) — "a decent amount" means a reasonable, satisfying amount; slightly less formal.
  • Respectable — implies the size deserves recognition; e.g., "a respectable sum."
  • Modest — be careful, this is almost an antonym; "a modest amount" means a small or restrained amount.

Among all of these, considerable and substantial are the closest to "sizable" in everyday use.
Words that mean the opposite (antonyms)

• Tiny, small, little
  • Negligible — so small it does not matter
  • Minimal — reduced to the least possible
  • Insignificant — too small to deserve notice
  • Meager — disappointingly small; barely enough
  • Modest — small and restrained
The most natural word pairings (collocations)

In practice, "sizable" is most often heard before these kinds of words:

  • sizable amount / sum / chunk
  • sizable number / portion / share
  • sizable crowd / group / audience
  • sizable profit / loss / return
  • sizable difference / gap
  • sizable investment / contribution / donation
  • sizable majority / minority
  • sizable collection / inventory / reserve
Quick spelling note

You may see two spellings in books and articles:

  • Sizable — standard in American English
  • Sizeable — standard in British English

Both are entirely correct. Neither one is wrong.
The one-sentence summary to anchor it all
"Sizable" means notably large — large enough that it deserves to be taken seriously — but not necessarily the largest thing possible, and always measured relative to what is normal in that context.
14641:
To size up something or someone means to carefully look at, assess, and form a judgment about them — usually so you know how to deal with them.

It is not just a quick glance. It is a deliberate, thoughtful observation where you are actively trying to understand what you are dealing with.

Think of it like this: a tailor "sizes up" a customer to understand their measurements before stitching a suit. In everyday English, we borrowed that idea and stretched it — now we "size up" not just objects, but people, situations, problems, and challenges. We are trying to measure their true nature.
A Concrete Image to Remember It By

Imagine a lion watching a herd of deer before it decides to hunt. It is not just staring blankly — it is studying which deer is weakest, which is closest, which direction they might run. It is making a calculated judgment.

That careful, deliberate evaluation — that is sizing something up.
The Different Ways It Is Used

1. Sizing up a person

This is the most common use. When you size up a person, you are observing them closely and trying to understand their character, strength, intentions, or abilities.

  • "The moment he walked into the room, she began to size him up."
  • "The interviewer sized up the candidate as soon as she sat down."
  • "The two wrestlers stared at each other, sizing each other up before the match."

Notice that in all these sentences, someone is carefully studying another person to form an opinion — often to decide: Can I trust this person? Are they a threat? Are they capable?

2. Sizing up a situation

You can also size up a situation, a problem, or a challenge — meaning you assess how difficult, complex, or serious it is before acting.

  • "The firefighter arrived at the scene and quickly sized up the situation."
  • "Before making any decision, take a moment to size up what you are dealing with."
  • "She sized up the problem and realized it would take at least a week to fix."

Here, the judgment is not about a person — it is about understanding the nature and scale of a challenge.

3. Sizing up the competition

In business, sports, or any competitive scenario, you might size up your rivals — meaning you study them carefully to understand their strengths and weaknesses.

  • "Before launching their product, the company spent months sizing up the competition."
  • "The chess player sized up his opponent's style of play and adjusted his strategy."
The Feel and Tone of the Phrase

This phrase carries a slightly strategic and watchful feeling. When someone "sizes something up," they are not being casual — there is a purpose behind it. They are gathering information so they can make a smart decision.

It also often implies a slight sense of caution or calculation, like you are deciding whether something is a threat, an opportunity, or a worthy challenge.

The phrase is neutral to informal in tone — perfectly natural in everyday conversation, journalism, storytelling, and speech. It is not rude or negative on its own, though context can give it a suspicious edge (for example, a thief "sizing up" a target has a darker connotation than an employer "sizing up" a job applicant).

"Size up" is a phrasal verb — that means it is a verb ("size") combined with a small word ("up") that together form one meaning. The two words cannot be separated in meaning: "size" alone does not mean the same thing.

How to use it in a sentence:

You can place the object (the person or thing being assessed) in two positions:

Option A — object comes after "up":
"She sized up the opponent."

Option B — object comes between "size" and "up":
"She sized the opponent up."

Both are correct. However, when the object is a pronoun (him, her, it, them), it almost always goes between the two words:

✅ "She sized him up."
❌ "She sized up him." — this sounds unnatural.

For regular nouns, both positions work:
✅ "He sized up the situation."
✅ "He sized the situation up."

Forms of the verb:

  • Simple present: "I size up every new challenge I face."
  • Simple past: "She sized him up immediately."
  • Present continuous: "He is sizing up his competitors."
  • Noun form: There is no commonly used noun form like "a size-up." You would say "an assessment" or "an evaluation" instead.

Do not confuse "size up" with its literal opposite — sizing up something to a larger size (like getting a bigger pair of shoes). In a clothing or retail context, "size up" can literally mean to go one size larger:

"These shoes are tight — I should size up."

This is a completely separate usage. Context will always make it clear which meaning is intended. If someone says, "I sized up my competitor," they are assessing them — not making them physically larger. If someone says, "I sized up in jeans," they bought a larger size.

In all the other contexts we have discussed (people, situations, challenges), "size up" means to assess and judge.
Related Expressions (The Same Family of Ideas)

Understanding related phrases helps you see where "size up" sits in the language:

"Take the measure of" — formal and literary, same meaning.
"He took the measure of his enemy and found him formidable."

"Weigh up" — to carefully consider something's pros, cons, and nature.
"She weighed up her options before deciding."

"Scope out" — to informally check something out before acting.
"Let's scope out the venue before the event."

"Sum up" — to briefly state a final conclusion about something (slightly different — this is about expressing a conclusion, while "size up" is about the process of forming one).

"Take stock of" — to pause and carefully assess a situation, usually your own.
"After the setback, he took stock of where he stood."

Among all these, "size up" is the one that most strongly carries the feeling of watchful, tactical evaluation — especially of other people.
A Few More Natural Examples in Context

• "As a nurse, she was trained to size up a patient's condition within the first few seconds."
  • "The two rivals had been sizing each other up for years, waiting for the right moment to compete directly."
  • "I could tell she was sizing me up during the entire conversation — deciding whether to trust me."
  • "A good general sizes up the terrain before moving his troops."
  • "He walked into the unfamiliar city, trying to size up the neighborhood before nightfall."
The One-Line Summary to Keep in Mind

"Size up" = look carefully at someone or something, assess what you are dealing with, and form a judgment — usually to decide how to respond.

Every time you see or hear this phrase, that is what it is doing: someone is studying something deliberately, with purpose, to understand it.
14642:
To skedaddle means to leave somewhere quickly, usually to avoid a person, a situation, or some kind of trouble. Think of it as a more colorful, energetic way of saying "run away" or "hurry off."

But knowing just the definition is not enough — the feel of the word is just as important as its meaning.

Skedaddle is an informal, conversational word, and it almost always has a playful or lighthearted quality to it. It is rarely used in truly serious or dangerous situations. If someone escapes a burning building, you would say they fled — not that they skedaddled. But if a child bolts out of the kitchen the moment they see it's time to do chores, skedaddled is perfect. The word carries a slight sense of humor and affection. It can even make the act of running away sound a little comical.
What makes it different from just "run away"

A few things. First, skedaddle suggests the departure is sudden and hasty — the person doesn't think twice, they just go. Second, it often implies the person is trying to avoid something: a task, a question, an awkward conversation, or someone in authority. Third, the way they leave is often a little undignified or chaotic — not a clean, graceful exit, but a scrambling, hurried one.

So while "run away" is neutral and factual, skedaddle paints a more vivid picture: someone rushing off in a slightly flustered, hurried, and perhaps cowardly way.

One very common use of skedaddle is as a direct command, the way you'd tell someone — often a child or a pet — to go away or clear out. When a parent says "Okay, skedaddle!" to a group of noisy kids, it means "go on, get out of here now." It sounds firm but not harsh — there's warmth in it.

The cat skedaddled the moment it heard the vacuum cleaner turn on.

He skedaddled out of the office before his boss could pile more work on him.

The kids skedaddled as soon as they saw the teacher walking over.

I knew the conversation was about to get awkward, so I skedaddled.

"Dinner's almost ready — skedaddle and go wash your hands!"

Because of its playful and informal nature, skedaddle doesn't belong in serious, formal, or tragic contexts. You wouldn't use it to describe soldiers retreating in a war, or someone fleeing in real danger. In those moments, words like flee, escape, bolt, or evacuate are more appropriate. Skedaddle lives in the lighter, more humorous end of the language.

Skedaddle means to hurry away suddenly, usually to avoid something — and it does so with a wink. It's the word you reach for when running away is a little funny, a little cowardly, or just a little rushed. It's casual, warm, vivid, and always informal.
14643: "Skein" has three distinct meanings as a noun. The first is the most common and concrete; the second is a specialized collective noun; the third is figurative. You will encounter all three in good writing, so understanding each one matters.
Meaning 1: A Loose Coil of Yarn or Thread

This is the word's most everyday meaning.

When yarn (or thread, or wool) is prepared for sale or storage, it isn't always wound into a tight ball. Instead, it is often wound into a long, loose loop — imagine winding yarn around your elbow and hand again and again until you have a big floppy oval of yarn. That loop is then gently twisted on itself or tied loosely so it doesn't fall apart. That thing — that loose, oblong coil of yarn — is a skein.

If you've ever walked into a craft store and seen yarn hanging on pegs in soft, floppy bundles, those are skeins.

The key idea: A skein is loose and looped, not tight and round. This is what sets it apart from a ball of yarn (which is tightly wound into a sphere) or a spool (which is wound around a hard cylinder). A skein has a relaxed, almost messy elegance to it.

"She pulled a skein of blue wool from her basket and began to unwind it."

The word also extends to other long, thin, flexible materials — a skein of silk, a skein of wire — whenever they are wound into that same loose, looped form. But yarn is the most classic and common use.
Meaning 2: A Flock of Wild Geese (or Ducks) in Flight

This is a collective noun — a word used to name a group of a particular animal doing a particular thing.

A skein is the specific word for a group of wild geese (or sometimes ducks) flying together through the sky, especially in that familiar V-shape or wavering diagonal line you might see on a cold autumn morning. It's only used when the birds are in flight. When the same geese are on the ground or water, you'd use different collective nouns (a gaggle, for geese on the ground). The moment they take to the air in a group, they become a skein.

"A skein of geese moved silently across the grey November sky."

This meaning paints a beautiful picture: think of that long, undulating line of birds stretching across the horizon. You can almost see why the same word applies to a long coil of yarn — both have that sense of something stretched out, flowing, and loosely connected.
Meaning 3: A Tangled or Complex Web of Things (Figurative)

In its figurative sense, a skein refers to a complicated, intertwined, and often hard-to-separate mass of things — events, lies, problems, relationships, or ideas.

Think of what happens when a real skein of yarn gets tangled. The threads run in and out of each other, and it's difficult to tell where one ends and another begins. That image is exactly what this figurative meaning borrows.

Writers use it to describe situations, stories, or sets of facts that are intricate, layered, and knotted together:

"The detective slowly unraveled the skein of deception that had kept the truth hidden for twenty years."

"The novel traces a skein of events that stretches from London in 1940 to Cairo in 1952."

The implication is always one of complexity and interconnection — things that are woven through each other, not simple or separate. There's also often a subtle sense that this complexity is somewhat difficult to untangle, just like a real skein of yarn that has gone wrong.
How the Three Meanings Are Connected

The figurative meaning borrows directly from the physical one. Once you know that a skein of yarn is a looping, winding, intertwined thing, you immediately understand why a "skein of lies" feels tangled and hard to unravel, and why a "skein of geese" evokes a long, flowing, connected line across the sky. The meanings aren't random — they radiate outward from a single central image: something long, looping, and interwoven.

Concrete (most common)A loose, looped coil of yarn, thread, or similar material
Collective nounA group of wild geese or ducks in flight
FigurativeA tangled, complex, intertwined web of events, lies, or ideas

The word carries a gentle, slightly literary feel. You'll find it more often in careful, descriptive writing than in casual conversation — but when you do encounter it, you'll now know exactly what it means in any of its forms.
14644: The adjective skeletal comes from the word skeleton — the framework of bones inside a human or animal body. Think of a skeleton: it is dry, bare, stripped of everything — no flesh, no skin, no organs. Just the bones. This core image drives all the meanings of skeletal.

The most direct meaning is simply of or relating to the skeleton. When doctors, scientists, or textbooks talk about the body's bone structure, they use this word.

"The X-ray revealed skeletal damage in the patient's spine."
"The human skeletal system consists of 206 bones."
"Skeletal muscles are the ones attached to bones that help you move."

Here, skeletal is a neutral, technical word. It just means: having to do with bones or the skeleton.
Meaning 2: Resembling a skeleton — extremely, alarmingly thin

This meaning describes a living person or creature who is so thin that they look like a skeleton wearing skin. You can almost see the bones. It is not just "slim" or "thin" — skeletal implies a disturbing, unhealthy, severe degree of thinness.

"After months of illness, he had become skeletal — his cheeks hollow, his ribs visible."
"The rescue workers found a skeletal dog abandoned in the warehouse."
"Photographs from the famine showed skeletal children with swollen stomachs."

This use always carries a tone of shock, concern, or sadness. It is the visual equivalent of saying someone looks like they are barely alive — just bones, almost no body left.
Meaning 3: Stripped down to the bare minimum — just the basic framework

This is the figurative (extended/metaphorical) use, and it is very common in everyday English. Just as a skeleton is the bare inner frame of a body, skeletal can describe anything that has only the most basic, essential parts — with everything else missing, removed, or not yet added.

"She presented a skeletal outline of her novel — just the main plot points, no details yet."
"After budget cuts, only a skeletal staff remained to run the office."
"The architect showed us the skeletal frame of the building before construction was complete."
"The government's skeletal plan lacked any concrete steps."

A key phrase: skeletal crew (or skeletal staff) — This refers to the absolute minimum number of people needed to keep something running. Imagine a ship whose full crew is 50 people, but during a holiday, only 8 show up — just enough to operate it. Those 8 form a skeletal crew. The word captures the idea of "barely enough to function."

In this figurative sense, skeletal is not necessarily negative — it often just means preliminary, stripped down, or bare-bones. A writer might show a skeletal draft to their editor before it's fleshed out. This is a neutral or even practical use.
The unifying idea behind all three meanings

Every use of skeletal points back to the same central image: the skeleton as a bare, stripped-down framework — the minimum that remains when everything else is gone.

  • In anatomy → relating to that framework of bones
  • In appearance → so thin you look like that bare framework
  • In structure/plan/quantity → reduced to only the bare framework, nothing extra

• In the anatomical sense: neutral and technical.
  • In the thinness sense: strong, alarming, emotional. Using this word implies something is wrong — it is rarely a compliment.
  • In the figurative sense: neutral to mildly negative, depending on context. A skeletal outline is simply unfinished. A skeletal response from a government might suggest inadequacy or laziness.
A few more natural examples to sharpen your understanding

"The old mansion was now just a skeletal ruin — only the stone walls still stood."
(Nothing remains except the bare structure — like a skeleton.)

"The director approved a skeletal budget for the film."
(Barely enough money — the absolute minimum.)

"Survivors of the shipwreck were skeletal when they were finally rescued."
(Severely, shockingly thin — wasted away to almost nothing.)

"The company operates with a skeletal workforce during the holidays."
(The minimum number of employees needed to keep things going.)

SenseWhat it meansTone

In one sentence each:

  • Anatomical: relating to the skeleton or bones.
  • Physical appearance: so thin that the person or creature looks like a skeleton.
  • Figurative: stripped down to only the essential bare frame — the absolute minimum of something.

Whenever you see skeletal, ask yourself: Is this talking about bones? About thinness? Or about something reduced to its bare minimum? One of those three meanings will almost always apply, and the context will make it obvious which one.
14645:
A skeptic is a person who does not simply accept a claim, belief, or idea just because someone says it is true. Instead, a skeptic pauses, questions it, and asks: "What is the evidence for this? Does this actually make sense? Why should I believe it?"

Think of a skeptic as someone with an internal filter. Before any new idea passes through that filter and gets accepted as true, it has to earn its place by surviving questioning and scrutiny.

Imagine someone tries to sell you a pill and says, "This cures any disease in 24 hours!"

Most people might be impressed and believe it. A skeptic, however, would ask:

  • Has this been tested scientifically?
  • What do doctors say about it?
  • Is the person selling it trying to make money off me?
  • Has anyone independently verified this claim?

The skeptic is not being rude or difficult. They are simply refusing to hand over their belief for free. They want it to be earned through evidence and reason.

This is very important, because skeptic is frequently misunderstood.

A skeptic is not someone who refuses to believe anything. That would be a cynic or a nihilist. A genuine skeptic is absolutely willing to believe something — but only once the evidence is good enough. Their mind is open, but not carelessly so. As the popular saying goes: "Keep an open mind, but not so open that your brain falls out."

A skeptic is not a pessimist. Pessimism is about expecting bad outcomes. Skepticism has nothing to do with optimism or pessimism — it is purely about how carefully you evaluate claims before accepting them.

A skeptic is not a denier. A denier rejects something regardless of evidence — they have already made up their mind and no amount of proof will change it. A skeptic is the opposite of this. A skeptic follows the evidence. If strong, reliable evidence comes along, a true skeptic will update their belief and accept it. Denial is closed-minded; skepticism is open-minded-but-careful.

A skeptic is not the same as a cynic. A cynic distrusts people and their motives (e.g., "Politicians only care about power"). A skeptic doubts claims and ideas (e.g., "I need to see the data before I accept this"). You can be a warm, trusting, kind person and still be a skeptic.

Skepticism is not one-size-fits-all. It exists on a spectrum.

Everyday skepticism is the most common. This is when an ordinary person doubts a specific claim in daily life. For example: "I'm skeptical that this new gadget actually works as advertised," or "I'm not sure that news story is accurate — let me check another source." Most thoughtful, careful people are skeptics in this everyday sense, even if they never use that word for themselves.

Scientific skepticism is a more structured form. A scientific skeptic applies the tools of logic and scientific method to evaluate claims — especially bold or extraordinary ones. The guiding principle here is famous: Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence. If someone claims that a common herb cures cancer, a scientific skeptic would require rigorous clinical trials, not just personal testimonials, before accepting it. Scientific skeptics tend to be particularly active in debunking pseudoscience, conspiracy theories, miracle cures, and paranormal claims.

Philosophical skepticism is the deepest and most radical form. Here, the skeptic questions not just individual claims but the very foundations of human knowledge itself. A philosophical skeptic might ask: "Can we truly know anything with certainty? How do we know our senses are not deceiving us? How do we know the external world is even real?" This has been a central subject in philosophy for thousands of years. Most philosophical skeptics are not claiming the world is an illusion — they use this kind of deep questioning as a tool to explore the limits and reliability of human knowledge.
The Strength of Being a Skeptic

Skepticism is considered an intellectual virtue, not a flaw. It protects you from:

  • Being misled by false information or propaganda
  • Falling for scams, miracle cures, or manipulative advertising
  • Accepting beliefs purely because of social pressure or authority
  • Spreading misinformation to others

Historically, skeptical thinking has been a cornerstone of science, medicine, law, and journalism — any field where getting the truth right truly matters.

The word "skeptic" carries a built-in balance that is easy to miss. A good skeptic is neither gullible nor dismissive. They do not say "yes" too quickly, but they also do not say "no" too quickly. They sit in the honest middle ground of "show me," and they are genuinely willing to be convinced by good evidence.

A skeptic is someone who demands good evidence and sound reasoning before accepting a claim as true. They question rather than automatically believe. They update their views when the evidence is strong. And they protect both themselves and others from the harm that comes from accepting falsehoods too easily. Being a skeptic is simply a commitment to thinking carefully before believing.
14646:
When someone is skeptical, they are not easily convinced. They hear a claim, a story, or an idea — and instead of immediately believing it, they pause and think: "Really? Are you sure? Where's the proof?"

A skeptical person requires evidence or good reasons before they accept something as true.
Breaking It Down Simply

Imagine your friend tells you: "I found a magic cream that makes you grow 3 inches taller in a week."

A non-skeptical person might say: "Wow! Where can I buy it?"

A skeptical person says: "I'm not sure I believe that. How does it work? Has anyone tested it? What does science say?"

The skeptical person isn't being rude. They're simply withholding belief until they see solid proof.
What Skeptical Really Captures

Being skeptical means sitting in a specific mental state — somewhere between believing and disbelieving. It is not outright rejection. It is a careful, questioning attitude that says:

"I'm not convinced yet. Show me more."

This is an important distinction. A skeptical person:

  • Has not decided the claim is false
  • Has not decided the claim is true
  • Is waiting for convincing evidence before making up their mind
The Spectrum — How Skeptical Can Someone Be?

Skepticism comes in degrees.

Mildly skeptical — You raise an eyebrow. You have a small doubt, but you're fairly open. Example: "Hmm, I'm a little skeptical that this new restaurant is as good as everyone says, but let's try it."

Moderately skeptical — You have significant doubts and want clear reasons before you believe. Example: "I'm skeptical that this diet plan actually works. I'd want to see real studies."

Deeply/Highly skeptical — You have very strong doubts and would need extraordinary evidence to be persuaded. Example: "I'm deeply skeptical that anyone can predict the stock market with 100% accuracy."
What Triggers Skepticism?

You tend to feel skeptical when:

  • A claim sounds too good to be true ("Earn $10,000 a day working from home!")
  • A claim contradicts what you already know from reliable knowledge
  • The person making the claim has a motive to lie or exaggerate
  • There is no evidence offered, only opinion or emotion
  • The claim is extraordinary and would require unusual proof
How It Is Used — Real Sentence Examples

• "She was skeptical about the new medicine, so she asked her doctor for more information."
  • "The scientist remained skeptical of the results until the experiment was repeated several times."
  • "I'm skeptical that he'll finish the project on time — he's always late."
  • "Many people were skeptical about the politician's promises."
  • "You should be skeptical of any news story that confirms exactly what you already want to believe."
Skeptical About vs. Skeptical Of

Both are correct, and the meaning is nearly identical. Use whichever sounds natural.

  • Skeptical about his intentions
  • Skeptical of his intentions

You'll hear both all the time. Neither is wrong.
Common Word Partners (Collocations)

These words and phrases are often paired with skeptical in everyday English:

  • Remain skeptical — "Experts remain skeptical."
  • Deeply / highly skeptical — stronger versions
  • Healthy skepticism — this phrase is actually a compliment (see below)
  • Raise a skeptical eyebrow — a visual expression of doubt
  • Meet with skepticism — when an idea is received with doubt by others
"Healthy Skepticism" — A Very Important Phrase

This is a phrase you'll encounter often. It means that some skepticism is a good thing. It keeps you from being fooled, manipulated, or misled.

A person with healthy skepticism doesn't blindly trust everything they read, hear, or are sold. They ask questions. They check sources. This is widely considered a sign of intelligence and critical thinking, not stubbornness or negativity.
Skeptical vs. Cynical — A Crucial Difference

These two words are frequently confused, so this distinction is worth knowing.

Skeptical = "I need proof before I believe this." → Open-minded, waiting for evidence, could still be convinced.

Cynical = "People are selfish and dishonest, and nothing is genuine." → A deeply negative, distrustful view of the world and people's motives; often not based on specific evidence but on a general bitter attitude.

A skeptic can be won over with good evidence.
A cynic often can't be won over, because their distrust is rooted in a general belief that people and the world are fundamentally bad or fake.

Skeptical is generally neutral or positive. Cynical usually has a negative tone.
Skeptical vs. Doubtful — Another Fine Distinction

Doubtful often leans more toward thinking something is probably not true.
Skeptical is more about wanting proof before deciding either way.

  • "I'm doubtful he'll come" → I think he probably won't come.
  • "I'm skeptical about his story" → I'm not ready to accept it without more evidence.

The difference is subtle, but skeptical is more about questioning and demanding evidence, while doubtful is more about leaning toward disbelief.
Related Word Forms

Since you're a learner, it helps to know the word family:

  • Skeptic (noun) — a person who is skeptical. "He's a well-known skeptic."
  • Skeptical (adjective) — the feeling/attitude of doubt. "She was skeptical."
  • Skeptically (adverb) — in a skeptical manner. "He looked at the offer skeptically."
  • Skepticism (noun) — the general state or habit of being skeptical. "Her skepticism saved her from being scammed."
The One-Line Summary
Skeptical means having doubt and wanting proof — you're not convinced yet, you're not blindly trusting, and you won't believe something just because someone says so.

Skepticism is the philosophical position that questions whether we can truly know anything — or at least, whether we can be as certain about things as we think we are.

The word comes from the ancient Greek word "skeptikos," which means "one who examines" or "one who inquires." So a skeptic is not someone who simply says "nothing is real" or "nothing matters." A skeptic is someone who says, "Wait — how do you actually know that? Have you really examined it carefully enough?"

Think of it this way: most of us walk through life taking thousands of things for granted. You assume the chair you're sitting on is real. You assume the sun will rise tomorrow. You assume the person you see in the mirror is actually you. Skepticism is the philosophy that grabs you by the shoulder and asks, "But are you absolutely sure? What's your evidence? Could you be wrong?"
The Core Problem Skepticism Is Responding To

Before diving deeper, you need to understand the problem that gave birth to skepticism.

Philosophers have always been obsessed with knowledge — real, rock-solid, undeniable knowledge. Not just belief, not just opinion, but actual, certain truth. The ancient Greek word for this kind of knowledge is "episteme" (which is why the study of knowledge is called epistemology).

The skeptic noticed something uncomfortable: almost everything we believe, we believe based on something that could, in theory, be wrong. Our senses can deceive us. Our reasoning can have flaws. Other people can lie to us. Our memories are imperfect. So if all our sources of information are potentially unreliable, how can we claim to know anything for certain?

This is the heart of the skeptical challenge.
The Two Major Traditions of Ancient Skepticism

Skepticism didn't appear as one unified idea. It grew through two major schools in ancient Greece and Rome.

1. Pyrrhonian Skepticism

The founder is Pyrrho of Elis (around 360–270 BCE), and this is the most radical form of ancient skepticism.

Pyrrho observed that for virtually every claim, you can find an equally strong argument on the other side. Is honey sweet? It tastes sweet to a healthy person but bitter to someone with jaundice. Is the wind cold? It feels cold to one person and mild to another. So who is right? Both experiences are equally real to the person having them.

Because of this, Pyrrho concluded that we should suspend all judgment — we should neither say "this is true" nor "this is false," because we simply don't have enough evidence to decide. The Greek term for this suspension of judgment is "epoché" (pronounced ep-oh-KAY).

Now, you might wonder: if you suspend judgment about everything, how do you live your life? How do you decide what to eat, where to walk, what to do?

Pyrrho's answer was: you simply follow appearances and customs. If food appears before you and looks edible, you eat it — not because you know it's good, but because that's how things appear. You follow social customs not because you've proven them to be correct, but because they're the default way of doing things. You don't commit yourself intellectually to anything.

The supposed reward for this total suspension of judgment was a state the Pyrrhonists called "ataraxia" — which means tranquility or peace of mind. Their thinking was: all human anxiety and disturbance comes from caring deeply about getting things right, from being emotionally invested in beliefs. If you let go of all firm beliefs, you stop worrying. You become calm. You achieve a kind of philosophical serenity.

Whether that's a desirable way to live is something philosophers have debated ever since.

The Pyrrhonist tradition was later carried forward and documented brilliantly by Sextus Empiricus (around 160–210 CE), whose written works are our best surviving source for understanding how ancient Pyrrhonists actually argued.

2. Academic Skepticism

The second tradition came from Plato's Academy — the school Plato founded — particularly under the leadership of Arcesilaus and later Carneades (around the 3rd–2nd centuries BCE).

Academic skeptics were slightly less radical than Pyrrhonists. They didn't say "suspend all judgment forever." Instead, they argued that while we cannot achieve certainty, we can still talk about things being more or less probable or persuasive. Carneades used the term "pithanon" (meaning "probable" or "plausible") to describe beliefs we can reasonably act on, even without certainty.

So if Pyrrhonism is like saying "I will never bet on anything," Academic skepticism is more like "I'll bet on the most likely option, but I'll never pretend to be certain I'm right."
René Descartes and the Most Famous Skeptical Thought Experiment in History

Fast forward to the 17th century. The French philosopher René Descartes (1596–1650) picked up the tools of skepticism — not because he wanted to remain a skeptic, but because he wanted to defeat skepticism and find something certain.

His method was called "methodological doubt" — he decided to doubt everything that could possibly be doubted, hoping that at the end, something undoubtable would remain. Think of it like shaking a bag of rocks and sand over a sieve: everything that can fall through falls through, and only what truly can't falls through stays.

He came up with three increasingly powerful skeptical scenarios:

The Dream Argument

Descartes pointed out: right now, how do you know you're not dreaming? When you're in a dream, it feels completely real. You don't realize it's a dream while it's happening. So how can you be sure your current experience of reading this isn't also a dream? If you can't rule that out, how can you trust anything your senses are telling you?

The Evil Demon (or Evil Genius) Argument

Descartes pushed even further. Imagine there is an all-powerful, supremely clever evil demon whose sole purpose is to deceive you. This demon could be feeding your mind false information about everything — making you think you see a world that doesn't exist, making you think you have a body when you don't, making you think that 2+2=4 when it actually doesn't. If such a demon existed, you would have no way of knowing, because all your experiences would feel perfectly real.

This is one of the most powerful skeptical arguments ever formulated. It shows that even our most basic beliefs — about math, about logic, about the physical world — are, in principle, doubtable.

(The modern version of this argument is the "Brain in a Vat" scenario, popularized in the 20th century: imagine you are just a brain sitting in a jar of chemicals, with wires connected to it that feed you perfectly realistic fake sensory experiences of a world that doesn't actually exist around you. How would you know?)

Descartes' Famous Answer: Cogito Ergo Sum

After doubting everything, Descartes realized there was one thing the evil demon couldn't trick him about. Even if he was being deceived about everything, there must be something doing the doubting. The very act of doubting is itself a form of thinking. And if he was thinking, then he must exist — at least as a thinking thing.

This gave him his famous conclusion: "Cogito, ergo sum" — Latin for "I think, therefore I am."

He had found something the evil demon could not take away: the bare fact of his own existence as a thinking being. From there, Descartes tried to rebuild knowledge on a firm foundation.
David Hume: Skepticism About Cause and Effect

Another giant of philosophical skepticism is David Hume (1711–1776), a Scottish philosopher who took skepticism in a different direction.

Hume argued that one of our most fundamental assumptions — that causes produce effects, that the future will resemble the past — cannot actually be proven. We assume that because the sun rose yesterday and the day before, it will rise tomorrow. But we've never proven that the future must resemble the past. We've just gotten used to it.

Hume called this the problem of induction. Induction means reasoning from specific past observations to general future predictions. And Hume said: we have no logical proof that induction is reliable. We just assume it works because... it's worked so far. But that itself is an inductive argument, which is circular.

This was deeply unsettling. It meant that not just our sensory experience, but the very logic of science — which depends on observing patterns and predicting future behavior — rests on an assumption that cannot be philosophically justified.

Hume also extended skepticism to our concept of the self. Most of us assume there's a continuous "I" that persists through time — the same "you" that existed as a child is the same "you" reading this now. Hume said: when he looked inward and introspected, he didn't find any stable, unified "self." He just found a constant stream of impressions, thoughts, and feelings, one after another. There's no separate "self" standing behind them. Just the stream itself.
Types of Skepticism

Skepticism isn't one single, uniform idea. It comes in many varieties, and it's important to understand the differences.

Global (or Radical) Skepticism

This is the most extreme form. It says we cannot know anything at all — not about the external world, not about the past, not about other people's minds, not about mathematics, not about morality. Everything is uncertain.

Very few philosophers actually hold global skepticism as their personal view. It's more often used as a thought experiment or a challenge to be responded to.

Local Skepticism

This is more common and more practically significant. Local skepticism doubts knowledge only in a specific domain, while allowing that we can know things in other domains.

For example:

  • Moral skepticism says we cannot have certain knowledge about what is right or wrong.
  • Religious skepticism doubts claims about the existence of God or gods.
  • Scientific skepticism questions whether scientific theories can be accepted as literal truth about reality (rather than just useful models).
  • Skepticism about other minds questions whether you can ever truly know that other people are conscious beings with inner experiences, or whether they're just physical beings behaving as if they have experiences.

Mitigated Skepticism

This is the moderate position, advocated by philosophers like Hume himself (despite how radical some of his arguments sound). Mitigated skepticism says: okay, we can't have perfect, certain knowledge. But we can have practical, workable knowledge — knowledge that's good enough to live by. We can have reasonable confidence in things, even without absolute certainty.

This is actually the position most working scientists and practical thinkers adopt, even if they don't call it that.
Key Skeptical Arguments You Should Know

The Problem of the Criterion

This is a classic skeptical puzzle. To know anything, you need a method or criterion for distinguishing true beliefs from false ones. But to know that your method is a good one, you need another method for evaluating it. And to evaluate that method, you need yet another — and so on, forever. You never reach solid ground.

Alternatively, if you just say "my method is self-evidently good" — you're going in a circle, assuming your method is good in order to prove it's good.

This leads to what philosophers call the Agrippa's Trilemma (named after the ancient skeptic Agrippa), which says that all attempts to justify a belief lead to one of three problems:

  • Infinite regress: every justification needs another justification, going on forever.
  • Circularity: you eventually use a belief to justify itself.
  • Dogmatism: you just stop at some point and say "this one needs no justification" — but why not?

None of these is satisfying. This is why the Agrippa's Trilemma is considered one of the most powerful arguments in skeptical philosophy.

The Argument from Illusion

Our senses regularly deceive us. A stick looks bent when placed in water but is straight when pulled out. Train tracks look like they converge in the distance but are parallel in reality. Colors look different under different lighting. If our senses can be wrong about these things, why should we trust them about anything else?

The Underdetermination of Theory by Evidence

This is particularly relevant to science. The argument says: for any set of observations or evidence, there is always more than one possible theory that could explain them. The evidence alone doesn't tell you which theory is the right one — it's "underdetermined" by the evidence. So how do you choose? And if you can't definitively choose, how can you claim to know which theory is true?
Major Responses to Skepticism

Skepticism is powerful, but philosophers haven't just surrendered to it. Here are the main ways thinkers have pushed back:

Foundationalism

Foundationalists argue that there are some beliefs that need no further justification — they are "basic" or "foundational." Descartes tried this with cogito ergo sum. Some modern foundationalists argue that perceptual experiences themselves (like "I seem to see a red apple") are foundational starting points, even if we can be wrong about what causes them.

Coherentism

Rather than looking for one foundational belief, coherentists say: knowledge is like a web. No single strand holds everything up, but the strands hold each other up collectively. A belief is justified if it coheres — fits together consistently — with all your other beliefs. The more beliefs fit together into a consistent picture, the more confident you can be.

Reliabilism

This approach, associated with the philosopher Alvin Goldman, says a belief counts as knowledge if it was produced by a reliable process — even if the person holding the belief can't articulate exactly why they know it. Our visual system reliably produces accurate beliefs about what's in front of us, so seeing-based beliefs count as knowledge. The evil demon scenario is an unusual case, not the normal one, so we shouldn't build our whole theory of knowledge around it.

Contextualism

Contextualists argue that the word "know" means different things in different contexts. In everyday life, when you say "I know there's milk in the fridge," you're held to a reasonable everyday standard of justification. In a philosophy seminar discussing Descartes' evil demon, the standard for "know" is much higher. Both uses of "know" are legitimate in their context. Skeptical arguments only succeed by artificially raising the bar in everyday contexts, which isn't fair.

Common Sense Philosophy (G.E. Moore)

The British philosopher G.E. Moore responded to skepticism in an almost cheeky way. He held up his hand and said: "Here is a hand. I know it is a hand. Therefore, the physical world exists." His point was: my certainty that I have a hand is greater than my certainty that any skeptical argument is correct. So if a philosophical argument leads me to doubt whether my hand is real, something must be wrong with the argument, not with my belief about my hand.
Philosophical Skepticism vs. Everyday Skepticism

It's important to distinguish between two very different uses of the word "skeptic":

Philosophical skepticism is a deep, systematic questioning of the very possibility of knowledge. It's a position about the foundations of what we can know, not a practical attitude toward specific claims.

Everyday skepticism is when you're simply suspicious of a particular claim until you see good evidence. When someone says "I'm skeptical that this diet pill works," they're not saying knowledge is impossible — they're saying "show me the evidence."

The modern scientific skepticism movement (associated with people like Carl Sagan and the journal Skeptical Inquirer) is closer to everyday skepticism — it's about demanding evidence and applying critical thinking to specific claims about the world, like UFO sightings, alternative medicine, or paranormal phenomena.

Philosophical skepticism is more foundational and more radical than this, though the spirit of critical examination is shared by both.
Why Skepticism Matters: Its Legacy and Importance

You might wonder: if total skepticism is unlivable (after all, you can't actually function if you truly believe you can't know anything), why does it matter?

The answer is that skepticism has been enormously productive as a philosophical tool, even if the conclusion of total skepticism is not adopted.

It led to the birth of modern epistemology. Descartes' skeptical method sparked an entire era of philosophy dedicated to figuring out the proper foundations of human knowledge.

It humbled human arrogance. Before Hume, many scientists and philosophers spoke with great confidence about understanding the universe. Hume's skepticism showed that even our most basic assumptions (like causation) rest on shaky ground, encouraging greater intellectual humility.

It shaped modern science. The scientific method — with its emphasis on testing, evidence, peer review, and willingness to revise theories — is in many ways a practical response to skeptical concerns. Scientists don't claim absolute certainty; they claim the best available explanation given current evidence. That's a skepticism-informed position.

It protects against dogmatism. Dogmatism means holding beliefs rigidly without examining them. Skepticism is the antidote: it forces you to constantly examine your assumptions and remain open to being wrong. This is invaluable in science, law, politics, and everyday life.

It revealed the limits of human knowledge. Skepticism has been a constant reminder that human beings are fallible, our instruments are imperfect, and our understanding of the world is always a work in progress — never a finished product.
A Simple Summary to Lock It All In

• Skepticism = the philosophical questioning of whether genuine, certain knowledge is possible.
  • It began in ancient Greece with Pyrrho (radical: suspend all judgment) and the Academy (moderate: accept what's probable).
  • Descartes used skepticism as a tool (dream argument, evil demon) and found one thing he couldn't doubt: "I think, therefore I am."
  • Hume extended skepticism to causation, induction, and the self.
  • It comes in global (doubt everything) and local (doubt one domain) varieties.
  • Key tools of skeptical argument: Agrippa's Trilemma, the problem of the criterion, the argument from illusion, underdetermination.
  • Key responses: foundationalism, coherentism, reliabilism, contextualism, common sense philosophy.
  • Skepticism's lasting value is not as a final answer, but as a discipline of inquiry — a habit of mind that demands careful examination of what we claim to know, protects against overconfidence, and keeps knowledge honest.

In other words, being a good skeptic — in the philosophical sense — doesn't mean believing nothing. It means thinking carefully before believing anything.

At the heart of the word "sketch" is one simple idea: something that is quick, rough, and not fully worked out. Think of it as the first attempt at something — a starting point rather than a finished product. When something is a sketch, it captures the basic shape or idea of a thing, but leaves out fine detail. It is enough to give you a clear sense of what something is, without being complete or perfect.

Hold that core idea in your mind as you read the different uses below — you will notice it runs through all of them.

1. A Quick, Rough Drawing

This is the most common and concrete meaning. A sketch is a drawing made quickly, usually by hand, that captures the basic shape or look of something without much detail or polish.

A painter, before creating a full painting, might first sketch the scene lightly in pencil — just enough lines to plan where everything will go. An architect might sketch a building on a napkin during lunch. A student in an art class might sketch a bowl of fruit before painting it properly.

Key qualities of a sketch in this sense:

  • Done quickly
  • Uses simple lines, not colour or fine shading
  • Rough around the edges — imperfect on purpose
  • Often a preparation for something more finished later

Example: She made a quick sketch of the mountains before starting the painting.

2. A Short Written Description

The word "sketch" also applies to writing. Here, it means a brief, rough written piece that gives you a general picture of something, without going into great depth.

The most common form of this is a character sketch — a short written description of a person that captures their personality, appearance, and nature in a few sentences or paragraphs. It is not a full biography; it is just enough to give the reader a clear sense of who that person is.

It can also refer to a short written outline of an event, a place, or a situation — something that paints a general picture rather than exploring everything in depth.

Example: The journalist wrote a brief sketch of the village — its quiet streets, old stone walls, and the smell of bread from the bakery.

3. A Short Comedy Scene or Performance

In the world of theatre, television, and comedy, a sketch is a short, self-contained comic scene or performance, usually no more than a few minutes long.

Unlike a play or a film that has a long, developing story, a sketch is brief and gets to its punchline or comic idea quickly. Comedy shows are often made up of many different sketches one after another, each with different characters and situations. This format is called sketch comedy.

Notice something interesting here: in this meaning, a sketch is not necessarily rough or unfinished — it is carefully written and performed. What it shares with the other meanings is that it is short and limited in scope. It does not try to be a full, expansive story.

Example: The comedy show opened with a hilarious sketch about two people stuck in a broken lift.

4. A General Outline or Summary

More broadly, "sketch" can refer to any brief, rough outline or summary of something — a plan, an idea, an argument, or a situation. When you give someone "a sketch" of something, you are giving them a general picture without going into details.

Example: He gave us a rough sketch of his plan before we discussed the details.
The One Quality That Ties It All Together

Whether it is a drawing, a piece of writing, a comedy scene, or a general outline, a sketch always shares these qualities:

  • Brief — it does not overstay its welcome
  • Rough or limited — it does not try to cover everything
  • Suggestive — it gives you enough to understand the main idea, even if the fine details are missing

A sketch is never the complete, finished version of something. It is a glimpse — sharp enough to be meaningful, but deliberately limited.

• A sketch is not a detailed painting or drawing — that would simply be called a drawing, illustration, or painting.
  • A sketch is not a full story or novel — those are complete, developed works.
  • A sketch is not a blueprint or technical diagram — those are precise and exact.
  • A sketch is not a thorough report — a report is full and detailed.
The Word Used in Common Phrases

• Rough sketch — emphasises that it is quick and imperfect (Give me a rough sketch of your idea.)
  • Character sketch — a brief written portrait of a person
  • Sketch comedy / comedy sketch — short comic performances
  • Thumbnail sketch — an extremely small or very brief sketch, either drawn very tiny or described in just a few words
A Final Way to Think About It

Imagine you are trying to explain what a friend of yours looks like to someone who has never met them. You do not have time for every detail — so you say: "She's tall, has short dark hair, always wears glasses, and has a very warm smile." That is a sketch. It is not a photograph. It is not a complete description. But it is enough — quick, clear, and useful.

That is exactly what the word "sketch" means, in whichever context you find it.
14649:
When you sketch something, you draw it quickly and roughly. You are not trying to make a perfect, detailed picture. You are just trying to capture the basic shape and feel of something — the essential outline — without worrying about every little detail.

Think of it this way: a photograph captures everything. A sketch captures just enough.

1. To draw something quickly and roughly

This is the most direct, physical meaning. When an artist sketches something, they use quick, light strokes to capture the general form of a subject — a face, a tree, a building — without fully finishing it. A sketch is almost like a first draft of a drawing. It is loose, fast, and unpolished on purpose.

Examples:

  • She sat in the park and sketched the old church.
  • He pulled out his notebook and sketched the outline of a bird he had spotted.
  • The designer quickly sketched a few ideas before choosing one to develop further.

Notice that the action is always fast and undetailed. Nobody spends three hours sketching. Sketching is the opposite of laboring over every stroke.

2. To describe or explain something briefly and roughly (figurative)

This meaning works exactly like the drawing meaning, but instead of using a pencil, you are using words. When you sketch something in conversation or writing, you give a quick, general description of it — the big picture — without going into every detail.

This is a very natural, everyday use of the word.

Examples:

  • The manager sketched the plan for the new project at the beginning of the meeting.
  • Let me sketch what happened so you understand the situation.
  • The professor sketched the main arguments of the theory before diving deeper.

In all of these cases, the person is giving a rough, brief overview — not a complete, thorough account. Just like a drawn sketch, it hits the highlights and leaves the fine details for later (or leaves them out entirely).

You will very often see sketch out used as a phrasal verb. It means exactly the same as the figurative meaning above — to outline or roughly plan something — but it carries a slightly stronger sense of planning or organizing ideas.

Examples:

  • Can you sketch out your idea so the team can understand it?
  • They sketched out a rough schedule for the trip.
  • She sketched out three possible solutions before deciding on one.
The One Essential Quality: Deliberate Incompleteness

The most important thing to understand about the verb "sketch" — in both its meanings — is that the roughness and incompleteness are intentional. You are not sketching because you lack the skill to do more. You are sketching because the goal right now is speed and overview, not perfection and detail.

This is what separates "sketch" from words like draw, paint, describe in detail, or explain fully. Those words suggest care and completeness. Sketch always suggests something quick, rough, and preliminary — a starting point, not an endpoint.

• With an object: She sketched the mountains. / He sketched the key points.
  • Without an object: She sat quietly, sketching. / He was sketching in the corner of the room.
  • With "out": They sketched out a proposal.
A Quick Way to Remember It

Sketching = capturing the big picture fast, without the fine details — whether you're holding a pencil or choosing your words.

Every time you see or use the word "sketch" as a verb, ask yourself: Is this person doing something quickly, roughly, and without full detail? If yes, "sketch" is the right word.
